title: Tazria: after a birth (Leviticus 12)
hook: a new mother's time apart and her offering mark a life-changing passage

segments.voice: Yesterday, kadosh: holy, set apart, right down to the dinner plate. Your line was holy in the everyday. Which ordinary act did you set apart? Today, a new portion, and a new life. Day three hundred ninety-five.

Ask anyone who has just had a baby how they are, and watch their face try to answer. Exhausted. Overjoyed. Sore. Terrified. Sometimes all four before lunch. The world goes on as usual outside, and inside the house, everything has moved. The next portion of Leviticus is called Tazria, from its opening verb: when a woman conceives. And before it turns to skin and sickness, it stops for one short chapter, only eight verses, to mark what happens to a woman after she gives birth.
screen: `EXHAUSTED, OVERJOYED, SORE.` → `EVERYTHING HAS MOVED.` → `TAZRIA: WHEN A WOMAN CONCEIVES.`

segments.voice: First, the time apart. After a birth, the mother enters a period of ritual impurity, called tumah, and then days of purification. For a boy, seven days and then thirty-three. For a girl, fourteen and then sixty-six. The Torah gives the numbers and not the reasons, and nobody knows for certain why they differ. Second, what tumah is and isn't. It isn't dirt, and it isn't sin. In Leviticus it comes from contact with the edges of life: birth, death, bodily flows. A priest burying his own parent becomes impure too. Many teachers read the mother's time apart as a recognition that she has just been to the very edge of life and back. It meant, in practice, a stretch of weeks when she didn't come to the sanctuary, and wasn't expected to. Third, the offering. When the days are full, she brings a lamb and a dove or pigeon. And then a line that matters: if she can't afford a lamb, two birds will do. Nobody is priced out of marking a birth. The Talmud asks why a mother brings a sin offering at all, and one answer is gentle: in the pain of labor, a woman may swear things she never means to keep. Fourth, the passage. Birth changes the mother, not only the household. Leviticus gives that change a time, a boundary and a ceremony, so it isn't just swallowed by the week. Today, Jewish communities mark births with a bris for boys, naming ceremonies for girls, and a blessing of thanks a mother can say in synagogue.
screen: `DAYS APART, BY THE CALENDAR.` · `TUMAH: NOT DIRT, NOT SIN.` · `A LAMB, OR TWO BIRDS.` · `A PASSAGE WITH A BOUNDARY.` · then, large: `BIRTH CHANGES EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a new parent. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has had a baby recently, or adopted one, or is about to. Or your own parents, the year you arrived. Think about what that season actually asked of them: the nights, the body, the fear, the joy. Then choose one small thing you could do this week. A meal left at the door. A message that asks how they are, not only how the baby is. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayers. The bell holds the time.
Tazria. When a woman conceives: the portion that opens by marking a mother's passage after birth, with time apart and an offering anyone can afford.
Your line: birth changes everything. Today, ask one parent how they are, and wait for a real answer. Day three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Jewish communities mark a birth with a brit milah for a boy on the eighth day and a naming for a girl, often at the Torah reading or a simchat bat; in many communities a mother says Birkat Hagomel, the blessing of thanks after danger, when she returns to synagogue.

myth: Leviticus 12 calls a new mother sinful
tumah is ritual impurity from the edges of life, not sin. even a priest burying a parent has it.
a poor mother could bring two birds instead of a lamb
the text makes room so no one is priced out.
the Torah explains why the days differ for a boy and a girl
it gives the numbers, not the reasons.

fork.setup: the days of purification are over. a new mother is supposed to bring a lamb, but she can't afford one. what does Leviticus say?
options: she brings two turtledoves or pigeons.
fork.reveal: two birds will do. the offering is scaled so every mother can mark the passage.

original.note: Hebrew: "(when a woman) conceives", literally brings forth seed: the portion's first key word.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old rule that calls new mothers unclean.
what it means: a marked time apart for a woman who has been to the edge of life and back.
what a scholar hears: tumah in Leviticus attaches to birth, death and bodily flows, not to sin; the sin offering puzzled the rabbis, and Niddah 31b offers the answer about vows in labor.

notes: Numbers checked against Lev 12: boy 7 + 33 days, girl 14 + 66; offering a lamb and a pigeon or turtledove; two birds if she cannot afford a lamb (12:8).
Niddah 31b's answer (Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: in labor she swears she will not be with her husband again) is softened to 'may swear things she never means to keep'; confirm this framing is fair.
'Many teachers read the time apart as recognition of having been at the edge of life' is a modern interpretation, presented as such.
Birkat Hagomel after childbirth: customs vary between communities; confirm the howItsDone wording.
